tlds._doc: .com re-added to approved on 2026-05-26 after the OVH KS-6 migration (128 GB RAM, 16-core EPYC 7351p) validated 5 consecutive clean natural-cron runs 2026-05-22 → 2026-05-26 on the new architecture (Phase 4 snapshot classifier, RDAP 429 cooldown handling, keyword denylist Round 1, per-TLD display cap). Pre-.com memory_peak holds at 3.87 GB; .com parse is expected to push to 15-25 GB during set-build, still well within budget. Cold-start handled by scripts/diff.py — first .com run writes the R2 baseline only (0 drops reported); first real .com diff lands 2026-05-28. The original 2026-05-10 OOM that forced .com to pending happened on the 16 GB GHA runner; that hardware constraint is gone now that the pipeline runs on the dedicated OVH host. .shop moved to pending on 2026-06-01: GMO RDAP IP-block (rdap.gmoregistry.net rejects our OVH IP at the Cloudflare edge with instant 429), whitelist request pending with info@gmoregistry.com since 2026-05-30. Today's run spent ~45 min (09:43–10:27) fighting GMO 429 cooldowns and produced 0 available / 23 not_available / 275 unknown from the bucket; temporary removal stops the daily time bleed. Re-add to approved when the whitelist is granted — verified via IANA RDAP bootstrap that .shop is the only currently-approved TLD routed through rdap.gmoregistry.net (the other 45 GMO-served TLDs are brand/geo TLDs we don't have CZDS access to). Carryover .shop entries already in daily-domains.json will age out naturally over the 14-day rolling window; no backfill needed.

scoring_weights._doc: Relative weights; the formula in score.py averages over POPULATED components only so missing fields don't drag the denominator. cc_source_domain_count joined 2026-05-14 at 0.30 — symmetric with wayback because PLAN.md frames both as historical-authority signals (wayback = temporal evidence the site existed; cc = link evidence others thought it mattered). Domains absent from the CC graph (cc_source_domain_count=null) are excluded from the average rather than penalized.

_keyword_lists_doc: Keyword blocklist with three REJECT categories plus one SOFT-SIGNAL category. (1) rejected_keywords: exact-match against tokens split on dots/hyphens/digit-letter boundaries. (2) rejected_keyword_prefixes: startswith() against coarse tokens (curated subset of unambiguous abuse stems — 'cam'/'tube'/'sex'/'slot'/'poker'/'pirate' are intentionally NOT here because their English-word overlap was the 2026-05-17 migration's whole motivation). (3) rejected_keyword_substrings (added 2026-05-24, Round 1): substring match on the apex label, for scam-vertical stems where real-world spam concatenates the keyword into a longer compound name with no separator and no digit boundary (richmendating, miraclepills, onlinepharmacy) — none of those reach the token matchers. Curation rule for this list: entries MUST be ≥5 chars and compound-specific enough that incidental English-word overlap is rare. Known minor FPs: 'dating' catches 'updating', 'pills' catches 'pillsbury' — accepted because such names rarely drop. ROUND 2 (2026-09-19): added betting, casino, gambling, viagra, escort after TWO compound-apex misses reached the LIVE published list — bettingmastertechnic.com and onlinecanadaviagra.net. Both stems were already in rejected_keywords, but that matcher is token-exact and a single-token apex never fires it. Candidates were measured against 44.5M real apex names from the zone snapshots, counting matches the existing matchers do not already reject: betting 5,490 new rejects / 0.3% false-positive (Bettinger, Bettingen surnames); casino 63,925 / 0.008% (Casino NSW businesses); escort 8,468 / 0.3% (medical and oversize-load escort firms); viagra 1,037 / 1.6% — the FP class is 'Olivia Gra...' (oliviagrace, oliviagraham all contain oli-VIAGRA-m), accepted as roughly the same cost as the known dating/updating FP; gambling 6,149 / 4.1%, where the FPs are gambling-harm NONPROFITS (problemgamblingcouncil.org). Gambling is the judgement call: it is already an exact-token reject, so problem-gambling.org is rejected TODAY and the substring only makes that policy consistent — drop this one entry to publish such names again, the other four stand alone. REJECTED after measurement, do not re-add: cialis (84% FP — speCIALISt, soCIALISt), steroid (68% FP — ASTEROID), opioid (public-health sites), phishing (25% anti-phishing orgs), webcam (tourism/wildlife cams). Tests pin cialis and steroid as forbidden additions. (4) soft_signal_keywords: do NOT reject — output.py reads them to force a 'Caution' verdict on dating/snake-oil/get-rich-quick/crypto-speculative names; 'dating' and 'hookup' are dead entries here as of 2026-05-24 (the substring reject fires first) but kept to avoid scope creep.

availability_check._doc: Per-host bucket caps for the RDAP availability stage, derived from a runtime budget. For each distinct RDAP host bucket, cap = floor(max_runtime_per_host_seconds * workers / effective_throttle), where effective_throttle comes from api_min_interval_seconds.rdap_per_host[host] -> rdap -> 2.0, and workers from rdap_concurrency.per_host[host] -> default_workers_per_host -> 1. Buckets exceeding their cap are random-shuffled (seed = today's date int) then truncated. global_cap is a safety net against pathological days where filter behaviour leaks far more survivors than expected; today's typical 14k lexical survivors fits below it. Replaced the prior length-asc trim (max_candidates_for_enrichment=1000) on 2026-05-04 — that heuristic biased toward already-registered short names without improving Wayback-signal density. max_runtime_per_host_seconds bumped 900 -> 2700 on 2026-05-05 to compensate for slower throttles after the ban events; per-host candidate volume stays similar (each bucket still wall-clock-bounded, now at 45 min not 15 min). Total RDAP phase wall-clock = max(bucket_runtimes) since all buckets run concurrently, so the slowest bucket caps total at ~45 min. NOTE: max_runtime_per_host_seconds is intentionally kept aligned with the top-level availability_budget_seconds (2700 s as of 2026-05-07). availability_budget_seconds is the global wall-clock deadline applied across the entire RDAP phase inside validate_availability(); when it's smaller than max_runtime_per_host_seconds, it pre-empts per-host completion and behaves as a guillotine (the bug 2026-05-07 surfaced — 1500 s was firing before any bucket finished its planned 2700 s). With both at 2700 s the global deadline acts as a redundant safety net rather than the binding constraint. 2026-05-09: Verisign (.com/.net) joined as a single shared bucket at rdap.verisign.com → 4.0s throttle (Mario's choice over agent's 3.0s recommendation given 70% blast radius if banned + undocumented Verisign rate-limit policy + ToS 'high volume automated processes' prohibition). Cap math: floor(2700 / 4.0) = 675 candidates/day for the combined .com+.net bucket — small fraction of expected ~30-35k daily lexical survivors but ban-prevention takes priority over volume on first deployment. Loosen to 3.0s only after 1-2 weeks of clean Verisign runs. Same date, GMO (rdap.gmoregistry.net) bumped 4.0 -> 5.0 defensively after 2026-05-09 cron logged 8 Retry-After:0 soft warnings — today's per-registry throttle audit flagged GMO as the most-exposed of currently-clean hosts; soft warnings argue for tightening, never loosening. Audit also established that 5 of 8 calibrated registries (Verisign, PIR, Identity Digital, GoDaddy/.biz, Radix) publish no numeric rate limit and rely on discretionary ToS enforcement; only CentralNic publishes a numeric ceiling (1800 q/15min = 2 q/s, /24 IPv4 aggregation). 2026-06-02: max_runtime_per_host_seconds 2700 -> 5400 (and the aligned top-level availability_budget_seconds 2700 -> 5400) — runs each bucket ~2x longer at the SAME pace to check more above-gate overflow per run. Per-host caps are derived (cap = floor(runtime x workers / throttle)) so this single knob doubles every host's cap proportionally: Verisign .com+.net floor(5400 x 1 / 4.0) = 1350 (was 675), GMO/identitydigital 1080 (was 540), PIR 1800 (was 900), Google/nic.biz 2700, centralnic/radix 5400. No throttle changed: the 4.0s Verisign interval and 1-worker-per-host concurrency are untouched — we run longer, never faster. The two values MUST stay aligned (see the alignment note above): availability_budget_seconds is the global guillotine and must not be smaller than max_runtime_per_host_seconds or it pre-empts buckets before they finish. Same date: STOP-ON-429 safety rule wired, then refined to a per-host 3-STRIKE rule (see rdap_429_strike_limit._doc): each 429 honors Retry-After and resumes the host; the host stops for the run only on its 3rd cumulative 429 strike. Other hosts unaffected; a 403 from any host is an immediate hard-stop + CRITICAL ALARM (catastrophic IP-block). See scripts/enrichment/_circuit_breaker.py HostStrikes/HostStop and rdap.check_availability. 2026-05-10: first Verisign-enabled run never reached the availability check — OOM-killed at 6m54s during the upstream .com zone parse. Root cause is in scripts/zone_parser.py, not in this stage: parse_zone builds a Python set[str] of all apex names in memory, and .com's ~160M apex names exceed the 16 GB GHA runner RAM ceiling (peak ~15.5 GB just for today_set; day-2 yesterday_set diff would push to ~30 GB). .com reverted to tlds.pending pending OVH KS-6 dedicated-server migration ordered today (128 GB RAM, 16-core AMD EPYC 7351p). .net stays in tlds.approved (~13M apex, comparable to .org scale, parses fine on GHA). The cap math in this _doc remains correct for all currently-approved TLDs; the OOM was a zone_parser memory-architecture issue, not a cap-math issue. .com returns to approved once OVH migration validates the pipeline runs cleanly at .com scale. 2026-06-07: max_runtime_per_host_seconds 5400 -> 7200 (and the aligned top-level availability_budget_seconds 5400 -> 7200) — one rung up the runtime ladder (45m -> 90m -> now 120m) after 3 consecutive clean natural-cron runs at 90m (2026-06-05/06/07) with 0 RDAP 429 strikes and 0 403 blocks. Same stepping discipline: raise ONE rung, then hold to warm Verisign over the next clean days before the next raise. No throttle/worker change — derived per-host caps scale proportionally: Verisign .com+.net floor(7200 / 4.0) = 1800 (was 1350), GMO/identitydigital 1440 (was 1080), PIR 2400 (was 1800), Google/nic.biz 3600, centralnic/radix 7200. Slowest bucket (Verisign) caps the RDAP phase at 120m; total run ~2.5h -> ~3h, leaving ~21h headroom before the next 09:00 UTC firing. The two values remain aligned per the alignment note above (budget must not be smaller than per-host runtime or it guillotines buckets early).

dns_check._doc: DNS pre-filter, run AFTER lexical filter and BEFORE RDAP bucket assignment. Queries NS records for each candidate apex via the system resolver (Quad9 since 2026-05-12 — see 'DNS resolver fix and DNSBL three-state contract' section in STATE.md). NXDOMAIN → dns_available=True → proceed to RDAP. Any NS records returned → dns_available=False → reject (the registry still delegates the domain, so it isn't actually available). Lookup error (timeout, transport failure, NoAnswer with name-exists-but-no-NS, NoNameservers) → dns_available=None → proceed to RDAP (fail-open, same epistemic-honesty pattern as the DNSBL three-state contract). Architectural intent: the RDAP throttle budget is the bottleneck on TLD scale-up — adding .com (~10× the next-largest TLD's apex count) would require either large RDAP throttle budgets (risks ban) or accept losing volume to skipped_budget. A genuinely-dropped domain has had its NS records removed at the registry, so a DNS NS query is a free, parallelizable pre-RDAP gate that should reject the 80-95% of post-lexical candidates that still have DNS infrastructure (in-transfer, in-grace-period, parked etc.) — letting RDAP focus its strict throttle budget on candidates that look genuinely available. Accuracy-preservation: candidates RDAP would have approved as available (404) have no NS, so DNS pre-filter rejects only candidates RDAP would have rejected too. Net effect: same final list, much less RDAP load. Defaults chosen 2026-05-12 (first deployment, conservative): 20 workers (~600 qps peak burst against Quad9 anycast — Quad9 publishes no formal limit but the DNSBL fix made them load-bearing for spam classification too, so don't poke them unnecessarily; raise later if production proves benign), 3s per-query timeout (covers slow TLD authoritative responses; the per-call wall-clock budget is workers × candidates × timeout / workers ≈ candidates × timeout but in practice dominated by sub-100ms responses), no throttle (set throttle_seconds > 0 if Quad9 fair-use starts biting). Set enabled=false to bypass the pre-filter entirely (escape hatch if dnspython misbehaves or Quad9 has an outage). Module: scripts/dns_prefilter.py — pipeline-stage helper, not an enricher (different lifecycle: runs once across all candidates with its own pool sizing; not registered in ENRICHMENT_MODULES).

cc_backlinks._doc: Common Crawl domain-webgraph integration. WIRED INTO PIPELINE as of 2026-05-14 — `scripts/cc_refresh.py` builds and uploads per-release artifacts to R2; `scripts/enrichment/cc_backlinks.py` is registered in ENRICHMENT_MODULES and runs as part of the daily enrichment phase. Strategy A (latest release only — see STRATEGIC_NOTES.md `Multi-release CC query strategy`). On first call per pipeline process, the derived SQLite for `latest_release` is downloaded from R2 to `~/.cache/domainsifter/cc/` and reused for every subsequent candidate (sub-ms point-lookups thereafter). `source_domain_count=null` from the enricher means 'domain not in this release's graph' — null-aware in score.py (excluded from average) and intentionally NOT counted toward `publish_min_enrichment_completeness` so absence from CC graph doesn't penalize a candidate at the publication gate. Accumulation strategy (REVISED 2026-09-20, see `refresh._doc_retention` - raw is now pruned, derived is still never deleted): raw vertices+edges (~10-18 GiB/release) live on R2 IA tier (S3-API class name `STANDARD_IA`, matches AWS conventions — NOT Cloudflare's Workers-API `InfrequentAccess` spelling, which 400'd on the first OVH run 2026-05-13) ($0.010/GB-mo, rarely re-read after derived build), derived SQLite (~1.5 GiB/release) lives on Standard tier ($0.015/GB-mo, read once per pipeline run). Year-end cost projection: ~$3/mo at year 1, ~$14/mo at year 5 (60 releases × $0.23/each). Schema: one SQLite per release with `meta` table (release, built_at, schema_version, source_url) and `cc_apex` table (apex_domain TEXT PK, source_domain_count INTEGER) — danglers included as count=0 for three-state symmetry (not-in-graph vs zero-inbound are different facts). Release column intentionally NOT per-row — file path encodes the release context, meta table self-documents. Refresh cadence: AUTOMATED as of 2026-09-20 - systemd/domainsifter-cc-refresh.timer fires weekly (Sun 18:00 UTC) into scripts/run-cc-refresh.sh -> `python -m scripts.cc_refresh --auto`, which discovers the newest release, no-ops when it is already installed, and swaps `latest_release` here only after the derived SQLite is verified in R2. The manual `--release <name>` path is unchanged and still works. See the `refresh` sub-block below for cadence, blackout, verification and retention; the STRATEGIC_NOTES.md `Common Crawl refresh cadence` open question is CLOSED by that block.

refresh._doc: Automated refresh of the Common Crawl release, added 2026-09-20. Before this, cc_refresh.py had no timer and had run exactly ONCE (by hand, 2026-05-13), while cc_source_domain_count carried scoring weight 0.30 - the data went 4 months stale and nothing alarmed. Driven by systemd/domainsifter-cc-refresh.timer (weekly, Sun 18:00 UTC) via scripts/run-cc-refresh.sh. CADENCE: Common Crawl publishes the domain-level graph MONTHLY as a rolling 3-month window (verified 2026-09-20 against commoncrawl.org/web-graphs: jan-feb-mar, feb-mar-apr, mar-apr-may, apr-may-jun, may-jun-jul, jun-jul-aug all exist for 2026) - the previously-recorded belief of ~3x/year was WRONG. Weekly, not monthly: discovery is a couple of HEAD requests and exits 0 as a no-op when the newest release is already installed, so a weekly tick costs nothing, picks a new release up within 7 days, and - crucially - RETRIES a failed or timed-out run next week instead of leaving it broken for a month.
refresh._doc_blackout: Refuse to start a multi-hour job inside the window where the daily pipeline (09:00 UTC, finishing 11:45-12:25) and the archive timer (14:00 UTC) own the box and the git push. Half-open interval [start, end). The weekly timer fires at 18:00 UTC so this never trips in normal operation - it exists to stop a MANUAL or boot-catch-up invocation from colliding with the daily run. pipeline_unit is a second, independent interlock: if that unit is active we skip regardless of the clock.
refresh._doc_verification: Gate on the derived SQLite BEFORE cc_backlinks.latest_release is swapped - a half-swapped release during a daily run would corrupt a day's scoring. Empirical baselines measured from cc-main-2026-feb-mar-apr on 2026-09-20: 124,646,710 rows, google.com 16,365,926 source domains, 16,875,725 danglers at count=0. min_cc_apex_rows is set to ~64% of that, loose enough for normal drift and tight enough to catch a truncated build. The canaries are LIVE PRODUCTION PROBES, not test fixtures - hard rule 1 (no real domains in sample data) governs fixtures, and the tests for this code use invented names against mocked SQLite. google.com is the canary because it is the single most-linked apex in the graph, so its presence with a large count proves the edges join actually ran; canary_absent proves we are not returning a count for everything.
refresh._doc_retention: R2 retention decision, 2026-09-20 - supersedes the 'never delete old releases' line in the parent _doc. RAW (vertices+edges) is PRUNED: keep the newest prune_raw_after_releases releases, delete older raw. Raw exists only to rebuild the derived SQLite, is re-downloadable from data.commoncrawl.org for free at any time, and is never read by the pipeline. DERIVED SQLite is NEVER deleted by this code at any setting - it is the durable asset (6.6 GB/release, and the only way a future multi-release strategy B/C or a backlink-trend signal could look backwards). Set prune_raw_after_releases to 0 to disable raw pruning entirely. Cost: raw pinned at ~21 GB IA (about $0.21/mo) instead of growing 10-18 GB per month; derived accumulates about $0.10/mo per release. The local SQLite cache under ~/.cache/domainsifter/cc/ is also pruned to the active release - at 6.6 GB per monthly release an unpruned cache fills the box.
refresh._doc_disk: Transient local disk the build needs, computed as (vertices + edges Content-Length from a HEAD probe) x this multiplier, replacing a hardcoded 25 GiB pre-flight check that was badly undersized. MEASURED on the box during the cc-main-2026-jun-jul-aug build on 2026-09-20: filesystem used went 11 -> 20 -> 49 -> 25 -> 29 -> 26.8 GB, i.e. a ~38 GB peak against 10.3 GB of raw = ~3.7x. Set to 5.0, not 3.7, because the sampling was coarse (5-min intervals over a 5m33s aggregate step, so the true peak is likely higher), and because the DuckDB spill scales with the edges file's ROW count rather than its compressed size - the previous release's edges were 18.2 GB against this one's 9.4 GB, so a future release could double raw and more than double spill. Overshooting costs nothing on a 467 GB volume; undershooting kills a multi-hour job at the aggregate step. The spill itself is caused by _DUCKDB_MEMORY_LIMIT=8GB in cc_refresh.py, which is deliberately conservative so behaviour matches a 16 GB dev laptop - a chosen disk-for-portability trade, NOT a bug to fix, and it does not shrink on the 125 GB box.
refresh._doc_staleness: Surfaced in the daily operational email by send_report.py. The 2026-09-17 lesson was that a silent multi-week degradation is the real failure mode, so an un-refreshed release must alarm on its own. CC publishes monthly; built_at older than this many days means at least one release was missed.

history._doc: Multi-release backlink history, added 2026-09-20. Answers the question Strategy A could not: what did this domain look like across the LAST SEVERAL Common Crawl releases, not just the newest one. Before this, R2 accumulated one derived SQLite per month forever and the pipeline read exactly one of them, so the archive was inert. DISPLAY ONLY at this stage - the history is emitted into daily-domains.json and rendered on the site, and it deliberately does NOT feed scoring. cc_source_domain_count keeps its existing meaning and weight (0.30) and its value is taken from latest_release exactly as before, so this change CANNOT move the published list or its ordering. Adding a decay signal to scoring_weights is a separate, later decision that wants real observed history to calibrate against - per the STRATEGIC_NOTES.md principle of proving the cheap thing before building the expensive thing around it.
history._doc_window: Releases are AUTO-DISCOVERED by listing cc/derived/ in R2 and sorting newest-first, then truncated to max_releases. There is deliberately no hand-maintained list of releases here: a manual list is exactly the kind of step that went four months un-updated and caused this whole work item. A newly-installed release therefore joins the history window on its own with no config edit. max_releases is the single lever that bounds LOCAL DISK: each cached derived SQLite is ~6 GB, so 6 releases is ~36 GB against the 467 GB volume, and the window grows by one release (~6 GB) per month until it hits this cap. Raise it deliberately, after checking free space. IMPORTANT for anyone reading a trend off this: consecutive monthly releases are ROLLING 3-MONTH WINDOWS and share two of their three months, so adjacent entries are NOT independent observations - at max_releases 6 there are only about two independent 3-month samples. Fine to display; do not fit a confident decay line to it. See STRATEGIC_NOTES.md `Common Crawl backlink history`.
history._doc_prewarm: Each release in the window must be present in the local cache BEFORE the 09:00 UTC pipeline needs it, or the first run after a new release lands would download ~6 GB inline during enrichment. The refresh path pre-warms the whole window right after a successful install (the same trick the in-R2 verification already uses for the active release), and `python -m scripts.cc_refresh --prewarm-history` does it on demand. Pre-warming is also why prune_local_cache must keep the WHOLE window and not just latest_release - pruning to the active release alone would delete the archive cache on every install and force a 30 GB re-download on the next run.

newsletter._doc: Daily newsletter draft generation via Buttondown. Enabled 2026-05-14 same-day as the wire-in commit — drafts are inherently safe (status=draft never reaches subscribers without a manual dashboard action), so flipping the flag on doesn't create deliverability risk. Idempotent: re-running the same day finds the existing draft by subject and skips creation. See STATE.md 'Daily newsletter — 2026-05-14' for the test-send workflow. Module: scripts/generate_newsletter.py — run-daily.sh invokes it AFTER pipeline.py succeeds, failure here is logged but never aborts the daily run. Disable by flipping enabled to false if Buttondown is misbehaving or for any reason draft creation should pause.
newsletter.intro_text: Today's top expired domain picks, sorted by score. Backlinks counts come from the Common Crawl domain-level hyperlink graph (release {cc_release}). All domains were available at last check — verify at registrar before buying.
newsletter._evidence_doc: Added 2026-09-19 for the first-ever send. featured_n picks render as rich blocks (reason + archived page title + signals) and the rest stay compact: a flat list of 20 equal rows gets skimmed and closed. The archived title comes from the wayback sidecar and is the differentiating content no competitor list has. excerpt_title_denylist suppresses boilerplate titles (Page not found, Home, Untitled) because showing those on a featured pick reads as filler and implies we checked something we did not; set it to [] to show every title. plaintext_api_field is OFF until the Buttondown field name for a caller-supplied text/plain part is confirmed - a wrong name is retried once without it, so a bad guess cannot cost the draft.

phase2._doc: LLM-based name-quality ranker (Haiku) inserted between the lexical filter and the RDAP availability check. Replaces the per-host random-shuffle trim with quality-ordered selection. Wires LIVE in tomorrow's production run (enabled=true on 2026-06-02). Fallback is wired to FAILURE ONLY — never to thin yield. Triggers: API error, cost-ceiling-hit-before-min-eligible, uncaught exception, missing ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Per product policy 'smaller but cleaner is better', min_eligible defaults to 10 so a thin-but-valid day publishes a short quality list rather than reverting to a longer mechanical one. Budget enforcement is two-layer: (a) planned, via target_n = floor(daily_budget_usd / cost_per_1000_planning_usd * 1000); (b) runtime, a thread-safe cost meter halts further batches at 95% of daily_budget_usd. Pricing constants in scripts/phase2_ranker.py PRICE_*_PER_MTOK; cost_per_1000_planning_usd is the BUDGETED rate (with retry-pass + drift headroom over the diagnostic-measured ~$0.19/1k). Overflow (above-gate candidates that don't fit any RDAP bucket) is persisted to R2 at state/phase2_overflow.jsonl with first_seen_date, aged out at 14 days — same rolling window as carryover. NOT committed to the repo: this is the public domainsifter repo and overflow is private pick-pool data. Tunable: daily_budget_eur (cap), score_gate (eligibility threshold), min_eligible (fallback floor — keep low to honor thin-but-quality days), batch_size (smaller batches reduce Haiku JSON truncation; 15 is post-diagnostic calibration). Diagnostic that validated the prompt + cost + quality lives in scratch/haiku_ranker_diagnostic/ (untracked).
phase2._claude_code_doc: Used only when llm.backend == 'claude_code'. Claude Code carries ~25k tokens of its own system prompt + tool defs on EVERY call, so the API path's batch_size=15 would be almost pure overhead; we chunk far larger instead. chunk_size 800 is set from a 2026-09-17 measurement on the OVH box: 29.4 output tokens per ranked name against a 32k output cap gives a hard ceiling near 1090 names/call, so 800 leaves margin for a verbose day. max_names_claude_code REPLACES the budget-derived target_n (daily_budget_eur / cost_per_1000_planning_usd), which is meaningless when inference is covered by the Max subscription rather than metered tokens; the runtime cost meter is likewise skipped on this backend. Both budget mechanisms stay fully active for llm.backend == 'api' so rollback is faithful.
phase2._chunk_size_note: Lowered 800 -> 300 after the first production run (2026-09-19) scored only 10,497 of 13,000 names. At 800 names (~24k output tokens) two chunks came back as malformed JSON and four stopped early — one returned 287 of 800 — and every unreturned name silently became below-gate without being judged. Shorter replies come back complete far more reliably. The cost is more calls (~43 vs 17), which is free on the subscription backend and runs llm.max_parallel at a time.

llm._doc: Backend selection for every pipeline stage that needs model inference (phase2_ranker, snapshot_classifier, classify_carryover). 'api' is the historical metered Anthropic path; 'claude_code' shells out to the `claude` CLI authenticated with a subscription OAuth token, costing nothing per token. Switched to claude_code on 2026-09-18 because the API credit balance hit zero on 2026-07-23 and will not be refunded. ROLLBACK is this one value. Implementation and the two traps it guards (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY outranks the OAuth token; a conversational refusal must not be mistaken for an empty result) are documented in scripts/llm_backend.py.

archive_generator._doc: Permanent per-domain reference pages (scripts/archive_generator.py), chained off a successful pipeline run via OnSuccess= in systemd/domainsifter.service. These pages are the site's ONLY long-tail SEO content; it produced 113 of them and then stopped dead on 2026-07-21 when the API credit balance hit zero, firing and failing silently every day since. Now runs on the shared llm.* subscription backend. sidecar_excerpts_path points at the wayback_excerpts.json written by pipeline Stage 4b: having the archived title/meta/headings is what lets a page state what the site WAS rather than speculating from the domain name, which is what the pre-2026-09-19 prompt did. timeout_seconds null defers to llm.timeout_seconds.
archive_generator._doc_excerpt_caps: Caps on the untrusted archived text persisted into each page's frontmatter. These MUST stay in sync with MAX_FIELD_CHARS / MAX_HEADING_CHARS / MAX_HEADINGS in src/pages/d/[domain].astro: the page truncates the same text again at render time, so a smaller value there would re-truncate what we already shortened and append a second ellipsis ('...…').

toxic_denylist._doc: Durable memory of every domain ever classified toxic, in private R2 at state/toxic_denylist.jsonl (never the public repo — it is a list of named domains we judge abusive). Exists because 'unknown' is BOTH 'not abusive' and 'the archive.org fetch failed', and verdicts were recomputed from scratch every run: on 2026-09-20 ridgemotorsports.net was correctly classified toxic the day before, came back 'unknown' when the fetch failed, stayed published and was given a permanent archive page — its archived content is an Indonesian online-slot gambling site. A verdict must not be erased by a transient network failure. Set enabled=false to neutralise the gate via config if a bad classifier run ever poisons the list; the pipeline then degrades to live-check-only, which is the pre-2026-09-20 behaviour.

snapshot_classifier._doc: Wayback-excerpt content classifier. Its 'toxic' verdict is the ONLY thing that trips the toxic gate in filter.keep_post_enrichment (scripts/filter.py). That gate has been open since 2026-07-23 because the classifier returned 'unknown' for every domain once API credits ran out. batch_size groups domains per model call (the old path made one call per domain, which is unusable against Claude Code's per-call overhead). shadow=true writes the verdict to snapshot_category_shadow and leaves snapshot_category='unknown', so nothing is evicted while we validate the new backend against the API-era verdicts; set false to arm it for real.
snapshot_classifier._shadow_armed_note: ARMED 2026-09-19 after the first live shadow run. The screen produced 29 real verdicts and flagged 3 as toxic: brightdawnnutrition.com (Chinese gambling site behind a nutrition name), languageidentifier.com (Chinese adult content), thegreenseason.org (a genuine African safari business whose pages were injected with Chinese lottery-gambling SEO). All three were verified correct by hand, and all three had been published to the live list because shadow mode meant nothing acted on the verdicts. None would have been caught by the keyword filter — the names are innocuous, only the archived CONTENT gives them away. Set back to true only to re-validate after a prompt or backend change.

display_caps._doc: Per-TLD ceiling applied at the DISPLAY layer only (homepage Today/Recent panels and the Buttondown newsletter top-N). Pipeline output daily-domains.json stays score-pure — this knob never touches the JSON contract. Rationale (2026-05-25): the published list is heavily .net-skewed because .net has Wayback content where other approved TLDs often don't. With ~232 entries across 14 TLDs and ~170 .net, a naive score-desc top-30 panel was rendering 25+ .net rows and creating an honesty gap against the 'curated across 15 TLDs' methodology copy. Algorithm: bucket by TLD, take top-N per TLD by score (slack flows naturally — TLDs with fewer than N just contribute what they have), flatten, score-sort, take panel size. Cap fires INDEPENDENTLY per surface: Today panel, Recent panel, newsletter top-N each see their own bucket. Tighten the cap (8→6) only if smaller TLDs still get crowded out; loosen (8→12) only if production data shows the cap is starving small-TLD slots without improving diversity. The newsletter and homepage may diverge later but share the same 8 for now (homepage panel=30, newsletter panel=20 from newsletter.top_n).

verdict_thresholds._doc: Tightened 2026-05-17. Promising used to be earned by score >= 40 alone; the tag became meaningless when ~all published rows wore it (89/89 on 2026-05-16). New bar requires significant historical web presence (wayback >= 1000) AND at least one external authority signal (OPR >= 1.5 OR CC backlinks >= 10). Candidates clearing only the score threshold demote to Caution instead. Clean (the top tier) is unchanged — score >= 70 wins. Soft-signal keyword matches (dating, snake-oil, get-rich-quick, crypto-speculative) force Caution regardless of the above. Verdict is computed in scripts/output.py:_compute_verdict and serialized as a JSON field — frontend and newsletter read it instead of recomputing from score (single source of truth).

api_request_timeout_seconds._doc: Per-enricher request timeout. Falls back to request_timeout_seconds when unset. Wayback CDX and crt.sh frequently take 15-30s under peak load — their 10s default forced ~80% of calls to time out on 2026-04-30. The retry-on-timeout logic in wayback.py / crtsh.py adds a second safety net.

rdap_concurrency._doc: Per-host concurrency for the RDAP availability check. The pipeline buckets candidates by RDAP host and runs each bucket in its own ThreadPoolExecutor; all buckets execute simultaneously. Within a bucket, workers serialize on the existing thread-safe HostThrottle so per-host request rate never exceeds api_min_interval_seconds.rdap (or rdap_per_host) — concurrency only ever fans out *across* hosts. Defaults are safe (1 worker per host); per_host stays empty until empirically validated against a specific registry. Lookup: per_host[host] → default_workers_per_host → 1.

api_min_interval_seconds._doc: Minimum interval between requests to each API host. With max_concurrent_enrichments=1 (sequential) and multiplicative 0.75-1.25× jitter applied per call, actual rates are ~25% slower than the nominal value. Tightened 2026-04-30 after 503/502 storms with the previous 1.0s/0.4s/0.2s settings. RDAP global default raised 0.4 → 2.0 on 2026-05-05 after multiple registries banned us (identitydigital 24h, PIR 1h) under the previous default — a new/unknown registry must default to a safe rate.

rdap_per_host._doc: Per-host overrides for RDAP. Falls through to api_min_interval_seconds.rdap when host not listed. Recalibrated 2026-05-05 after the first uncapped run produced multiple Retry-After bans: identitydigital.services 24-hour (1069 checked, 949 unknown), publicinterestregistry.org 1-hour (1966 checked, 1628 unknown), GMO 49 unknowns at 3.0s. Conservative empirical settings with safety margin — accept reduced volume in exchange for zero ban risk going forward, because a permanent ban from any registry would block the pipeline for that TLD entirely. Sources per host: identitydigital banned today → 5.0s (most cautious); PIR banned today → 3.0s (matches GMO caution); GMO 49 unknowns at 3.0s → 4.0s defensive bump; Google + nic.biz degraded but not banned → 2.0s; centralnic + radix clean at 0.4s but only 2250 candidates each so 1.0s defensive margin. 2026-05-09 changes: rdap.verisign.com added at 4.0s for the .com/.net rollout (Mario's choice over agent's 3.0s recommendation; reasoning lives in availability_check._doc). rdap.gmoregistry.net 4.0 -> 5.0 after today's cron logged 8 Retry-After:0 soft warnings; the per-registry throttle audit flagged GMO as the most-exposed of currently-clean hosts. Audit findings (5 of 8 registries publish no numeric limit; only CentralNic has a documented ceiling at 2 q/s with /24 IPv4 aggregation) confirm that calibration here is empirical-only for every host except centralnic.

rdap_429_backoff_floor_seconds._doc: Minimum seconds to wait after an RDAP 429 before the single retry, AND the per-host cooldown window during which further requests to that host are skipped without an HTTP call. Added 2026-05-22 after the GMO bucket logged a 47.6% unknown rate (257 unknown / 540 candidates) driven by a retry-during-cooldown cascade: the prior 1s+2s backoff retried entirely inside GMO's documented 60s cooldown, and GMO escalates non-compliance to temporary IP blocking. On a 429, scripts/enrichment/_circuit_breaker.py honors max(parsed Retry-After header, floor); GMO sends a useless literal 'Retry-After: 0' so the floor is what binds. Lookup: per_host[host] -> default. The gmoregistry value 60 is authoritative — verbatim from rdap.gmoregistry.net/help ('do not access any more for at least a minute to avoid temporary blocking of your address'). default 5 is a conservative small floor for hosts with no documented cooldown. This knob is ORTHOGONAL to api_min_interval_seconds (steady-state pacing): the 5.0s GMO steady-state throttle is unchanged — a 1 req/sec probe on 2026-05-22 confirmed GMO does not rate-limit at steady state, so the cascade was never a steady-state-rate problem.

_rdap_429_strike_limit_doc: Per-host cumulative 429 strike cap for the RDAP availability stage (added 2026-06-02, replacing the 2026-06-02-morning hard-stop-on-first-429 which was over-tuned — a single transient 429 retired a host's whole bucket). On each 429 a host gets one strike: we honor Retry-After (arm GLOBAL_HOST_COOLDOWN so subsequent domains skip during the window) and then RESUME querying at the normal per-host throttle. Strikes accumulate CUMULATIVELY across the bucket for the run (a success does NOT reset the counter), so clustered-but-non-adjacent 429s still count and spacing can't evade the cap. On the Nth strike (default 3 = sustained pushback) the host is STOPPED permanently for the run (GLOBAL_HOST_STOP) — results gathered so far are kept, the rest are left unchecked-and-unverified, other hosts finish, and we publish what we have. Per RFC 7480 §5.5 a 429 is the survivable 'decrease your rate' signal, not the catastrophic one; 3 strikes is the heuristic for 'the registry means it'. ORTHOGONAL to 403: a 403 (rdap.check_availability) is an immediate hard-stop + CRITICAL alarm with no strike accounting — one is enough, it is the catastrophic IP-block. Tunable without code; lower to 1 to restore hard-stop-on-first, raise for more tolerance. Counter lives in scripts/enrichment/_circuit_breaker.py HostStrikes (GLOBAL_HOST_STRIKES).
